Motiv: Hass auf DemokratenMörder von US-Politikerin Hortman kommt lebenslang in Haft
In Minnesota erschießt ein Mann die Kongressabgeordnete Melissa Hortman und ihren Ehemann und verletzt zwei weitere Abgeordnete schwer. Er plante wohl noch weitere Morde. Mehr als ein Jahr nach der Tat wird er verurteilt.
Gut ein Jahr nach dem Mord an der US-Politikerin Melissa Hortman und ihrem Mann Mark muss der Täter bis zum Ende seines Lebens ins Gefängnis. Der Bundesrichter John Tunheim verurteilte den Todesschützen in Minneapolis zu zwei Mal lebenslanger Haft plus 40 Jahren, wie US-Medien berichteten. Eine vorzeitige Entlassung des 59-jährigen ist damit ausgeschlossen.
Der Verurteilte hatte gestanden, die Demokratin Hortman und ihren Mann im Juni 2025 erschossen und zwei weitere Menschen schwer verletzt zu haben. Die Anklage hatte zuvor auf die Forderung nach der Todesstrafe verzichtet. Richter Tunheim sprach von einem "brutalen Angriff auf gewählte Amtsträger und ihre Familien". Er komme einem "Angriff auf die Demokratie" gleich, sagte er laut der Zeitung "Minnesota Star Tribune".
Täter wollte weiter morden
Der Täter hatte als Polizist verkleidet am Haus der Hortmans geklingelt und das Paar kaltblütig erschossen. Zuvor hatte er bereits den Politiker John Hoffman und seine Frau Yvette durch Schüsse schwer verletzt, beide überlebten jedoch. Nach einer aufwendigen Verfolgungsjagd mit Drohnen und 20 Spezialeinsatzkommandos konnte er schließlich in einem Waldstück festgenommen werden.
Melissa Hortman und John Hoffman saßen für die Demokratische Partei im Kongress des US-Bundesstaats Minnesota. Im Auto des Schützen fanden die Ermittler später eine Art Todesliste mit mehr als 45 Politiker-Namen. Nach Ermittler-Angaben war er offenbar ein evangelikaler Abtreibungsgegner und von einem Hass auf Demokraten angetrieben.
Die USA werden immer wieder von politischer Gewalt erschüttert. Der heutige Präsident Donald Trump wurde während eines Wahlkampfauftritts 2024 durch einen Schuss am Ohr verletzt. Im vergangenen September erschoss ein Mann zudem den Trump-nahen Aktivisten Charlie Kirk.

Vance Boelter sentenced to two life terms plus 40 years in killing of Minnesota lawmaker
In this handout provided by Hennepin County Sheriff’s Office, Vance Luther Boelter poses for a booking photo on June 16, 2025 in Green Isle, Minnesota.
Melissa and Mark Hortman were killed in less than 30 seconds on June 14, 2025, in a shocking act of political violence.
But their quick deaths are of no comfort to their son, Colin Hortman, who on Thursday told a federal judge that he falls asleep every night picturing a waterfall of blood flowing down the stairs of his childhood home in Brooklyn Park. It’s the same image he awakens to.
And his parents’ quick demise is of no comfort, he said, because the last thing his mother saw before she was killed was her husband and beloved dog shot multiple times.
Now, he has trouble recalling his parents without remembering the bullet holes in their bodies.
The horror of the assassination and the impact of the attacks on Minnesota’s political system were detailed by the Hortman children, Colin and Sophie, as well as 12 other victims at the Minneapolis federal courthouse, who shared how their lives were shattered by the man sitting next to them in an orange jumpsuit: Vance Boelter.
Boelter last month pleaded guilty to the murders of Melissa Hortman — the former Democratic House speaker and one of Minnesota’s most consequential legislative leaders — and her husband, Mark, as well as the shooting of state Democratic Sen. John Hoffman and his wife.
Thursday’s hearing signifies the final chapter in a year-long saga that has scarred the state and injected a new level of fear into politics.
U.S. District Judge John Tunheim sentenced Boelter to two consecutive life sentences as well as an additional 40 years. There is no parole in the federal judicial system, so it’s extremely likely Boelter will spend the rest of his life behind bars.
Tunheim said it’s the longest sentence he’s ever imposed on a person in the thousands of cases he’s heard over his career.
“I believe it’s well-deserved,” Tunheim told Boelter.
Boelter read a short statement apologizing to the victims aloud in court: “To every person I have caused loss, pain, heartache, confusion, sadness or loneliness, I am truly sorry.”
Boelter previously pleaded guilty to all the government’s charges: two counts of stalking Melissa Hortman and John Hoffman; two counts of murder in the killings of the Hortmans; and two firearms offenses in the shootings of the Hortmans and the Hoffmans, and the attempted shooting of Hope Hoffman, who managed to call 911 amid the bloody attack.
He admitted in court that he planned the murders months in advance, recording the addresses of his victims and buying a highly realistic silicone mask to impersonate a police officer.
In the early hours of June 14, Boelter drove to the Hoffman home and shot John and Yvette Hoffman through the front door. He then drove to Rep. Kristin Bahner’s home in Maple Grove, but she was on vacation. Then he drove to Sen. Ann Rest’s home, where he was seen by a real police officer who assumed he was a cop conducting a welfare check.
Next, he drove to the Hortmans’ in Brooklyn Park and parked his Ford Explorer with fake police lights turned on in their driveway. He rang the doorbell and said he was conducting a welfare check. He told Mark Hortman he needed to see Melissa, and then shot him. He shot Melissa multiple times as she tried to flee up the stairs. Boelter then shot her in the head.
U.S. Attorney for Minnesota Daniel Rosen wrote in the government’s sentencing memo that Boelter “expressed great disdain” for the Democratic Party.
“And he knew that the Minnesota Legislature was so closely divided that by killing four state legislators, the inevitable result would be a shift in the balance of power in both legislative houses,” Rosen wrote. “The astonishing damage that Boelter caused to his victims and to the State of Minnesota will never be cured. Justice requires that Boelter never be free ever again.”
Bahner was the first to read aloud her victim statement. She told Boelter she would have opened the door if she were home that day because she trusts law enforcement. She told Boelter that he failed his mission because she was still alive, and he has strengthened her resolve to continue advocating for her constituents.
John Hoffman, Yvette Hoffman and Hope Hoffman also addressed Boelter. Hope Hoffman criticized the media, who in the aftermath of the shootings, incorrectly reported that Yvette Hoffman jumped on top of her to save her from Boelter’s bullets.
John Hoffman read to Boelter several passages from the Bible, including Matthew 7:16: “By their fruit you will recognize them. Do people pick grapes from thornbushes, or figs from thistles?”
These, Hoffman said, are “words of the faith the defendant claimed to represent.”
He added: “(Boelter’s) actions spoke louder than any sermon he has ever preached.”
Many wiped away tears in the packed courtroom as legislators and family members told Boelter how his decision to kill their loved ones not only ruined their lives, but also irrevocably changed Minnesota.
J. Carroll Hortman, Mark Hortman’s father, said that his daughter-in-law Melissa was witty and brilliant. She had a bright future, and she had yet to experience the joy of becoming a grandparent.
“I believe she could have become the next governor of this state,” he said.
Mark Hortman’s family, including his brother and his sister, told the judge they were upset that Boelter’s guilty plea deprived them of a trial and of the opportunity to see Boelter receive the death penalty. They hated the idea that Boelter would live a comfortable life in prison.
Carroll Hortman said he blamed Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche, who he said did the country a disservice by agreeing to a plea deal. He also questioned why Brooklyn Park police on June 14 watched from afar as Boelter killed his son and went into the home and shot his daughter-in-law.
The Hortmans’ daughter Sophie Hortman said she had been working on her statement for the whole year since she lost her parents.
“I miss my mom. I miss my dad. I miss my best friends, and I miss believing in the goodness of humanity. The pain will never go away,” she said.
She also detailed the agonizing decision to put down the family dog, Gilbert, who Boelter shot multiple times before killing Melissa Hortman.
On the morning of June 14, Sophie and Colin received conflicting information about whether Gilbert was alive and went to the veterinarian.
A vet wheeled Gilbert into the room on a metal tray. Colin started screaming when he saw Gilbert. He had been shot multiple times, including in the head. Despite his condition, Gilbert still flickered his tail when he saw the Hortman children, and he gave them kisses with his big tongue.
The Hortman children asked the vet if he would let his own dog live in Gilbert’s condition. The vet said no.
“Colin and I agreed: Gilbert would want to be with his parents,” Sophie said. “I told him he would see mommy and daddy soon.”

sources.news_title: Vance Boelter Sentenced To Two Life Terms For Minnesota Lawmaker Shootings
sources.text:
Vance Boelter, the man who pleaded guilty to fatally shooting former Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband and wounding state Sen. John Hoffman and his wife last year, was sentenced Thursday to two consecutive life terms plus 40 years in federal prison.
WHAT HAPPENED
U.S. District Judge John R. Tunheim handed down the sentence in Minneapolis, calling it "the longest sentence I have imposed after hearing thousands of cases over the years," while adding that he believed it was "well deserved." Boelter, who turned 59 the day of his sentencing, pleaded guilty in June to six federal charges, including murder, stalking and firearms offenses, as part of an agreement in which prosecutors dropped their pursuit of the death penalty. The sentence carries no possibility of parole.
Prosecutors said Boelter, disguised in a tactical uniform and mask, arrived at Hortman's home around 3:30 a.m. on June 14, 2025, claiming to be a police officer conducting a welfare check. He shot Mark Hortman multiple times before forcing his way into the house and shooting Melissa Hortman, the former House speaker, as she attempted to help her husband. Boelter then drove to the home of state Sen. John Hoffman and shot Hoffman and his wife, Yvette, and attempted to shoot their daughter, Hope. In a pre-sentencing filing, prosecutors wrote that "justice requires that Boelter never be free again," describing his actions as "an assault on democracy" that "shattered the lives of his victims" and "threatened police."
Hoffman told the court that Boelter "looked me in the eyes and pulled the trigger" and "looked at my wife and chose to do the same," adding that he and his wife "now live with injuries" and "live with our bodies remembering the gunfire." Sophie Hortman, one of the couple's children, said her "entire life had been shattered in 30 seconds," while her brother, Colin Hortman, said the family went from "whole to shattered" in one night. Boelter apologized before sentencing, telling the court, "To every person I have caused loss, pain, heartache, confusion, shame or loneliness, I am truly sorry."
WHY IT MATTERS
The sentence closes the prosecution phase of a case that shocked Minnesota's political establishment and drew national attention to the safety of state lawmakers, particularly given Boelter's use of a fake police identity and tactical gear to gain access to his victims' homes. Judge Tunheim's characterization of the sentence as the longest he has imposed in thousands of cases underscores the exceptional severity with which the court treated an attack described by prosecutors as targeting the "organs" of Minnesota's representative government rather than a conventional act of violence. The extensive victim impact statements from both the Hortman and Hoffman families, delivered directly to Boelter in court, reflect the case's lasting personal toll even as the legal proceedings reach their conclusion. Minnesota lawmakers have separately moved to memorialize Hortman, including renaming a highway and the state's community solar garden program in her honor, signaling how the case has shaped the state's political memory beyond the courtroom.
WHAT'S NEXT
With sentencing complete, attention is likely to turn to any appeals Boelter's legal team may pursue, though his guilty plea limits the grounds available. Minnesota lawmakers are expected to continue discussions around legislative security measures in response to the attack. The Hortman and Hoffman families' public statements are likely to continue shaping conversations about political violence and lawmaker safety heading into future election cycles.

  -  In court Thursday, Sen. Hoffman said he and his family are constantly reminded of the extraordinary violence of that night, even in the mundane details of day-to-day life. -  Yvette Hoffman said she has been too traumatized to work since the attack in their home, and that she sees a therapist weekly. "I fought him, your Honor, with everything I had. And I finally got him out of our home. I will never forget looking down and watching my blood slowly stream down that white washing machine as I felt myself sinking to the floor," she said, barely holding back tears as she spoke. "We always have an escape plan now. This isn't how people should live."
                                        
 -  Boelter admitted in court in June that he spent months identifying and stalking his targets, before driving to their homes in the middle of the night, disguised as a police officer, with the intention of killing them.
-  Democratic State Rep. Kristin Bahner was one of two other legislators whose homes Boelter visited that night, but she and her family were on vacation. Bahner said the shootings had left her shaken. "I could not fathom why I was spared and (Hortman) was not," she said. "You failed because I carry her with me. In my mind and in my heart, she guides me."
-  "It is impossible to realize the damage that has been done not only to our family, but to our society," said Melissa Hortman's father Harold Haluptzok, who repeatedly referred to her as his "little girl." "I wish the perpetrator would have sat down and talked to Melissa about his political positions... if only he did that before he decided to kill them," he added.
-  Boelter also faces state charges, including two counts of murder, four counts of attempted murder, impersonating a police officer, and animal cruelty. The Hortman family's golden retriever was gravely injured in the shootings and had to be euthanized. Hoffman and his family filed a personal injury lawsuit against Boelter in April.
-  Boelter, who turned 59 on Thursday, has asked to serve his sentence at US Penitentiary Coleman II near Orlando, Florida, MPR News reports. Yvette Hoffman blasted the request in a Facebook post before the hearing. "The defendant is worried about his comfort," she wrote. "His victims lost their futures, and countless families will carry the trauma he caused for the rest of their lives."

Melissa and Mark Hortman were killed in less than 30 seconds on June 14, 2025, in a shocking act of political violence.
But their quick deaths are of no comfort to their son, Colin Hortman, who on Thursday told a federal judge that he falls asleep every night picturing a waterfall of blood flowing down the stairs of his childhood home in Brooklyn Park. It’s the same image he awakens to.
And his parents’ quick demise is of no comfort, he said, because the last thing his mother saw before she was killed was her husband and beloved dog shot multiple times.
Now, he has trouble recalling his parents without remembering the bullet holes in their bodies.
The horror of the assassination and the impact of the attacks on Minnesota’s political system were detailed by the Hortman children, Colin and Sophie, as well as 12 other victims at the Minneapolis federal courthouse, who shared how their lives were shattered by the man sitting next to them in an orange jumpsuit: Vance Boelter.
Boelter last month pleaded guilty to the murders of Melissa Hortman — the former Democratic House speaker and one of Minnesota’s most consequential legislative leaders — and her husband, Mark, as well as the shooting of state Democratic Sen. John Hoffman and his wife.
Thursday’s hearing signifies the final chapter in a year-long saga that has scarred the state and injected a new level of fear into politics.
U.S. District Judge John Tunheim sentenced Boelter to two consecutive life sentences as well as an additional 40 years. There is no parole in the federal judicial system, so it’s extremely likely Boelter will spend the rest of his life behind bars.
Tunheim said it’s the longest sentence he’s ever imposed on a person in the thousands of cases he’s heard over his career.
“I believe it’s well-deserved,” Tunheim told Boelter.
Boelter read a short statement apologizing to the victims aloud in court: “To every person I have caused loss, pain, heartache, confusion, sadness or loneliness, I am truly sorry.”
Boelter previously pleaded guilty to all the government’s charges: two counts of stalking Melissa Hortman and John Hoffman; two counts of murder in the killings of the Hortmans; and two firearms offenses in the shootings of the Hortmans and the Hoffmans, and the attempted shooting of Hope Hoffman, who managed to call 911 amid the bloody attack.

Bahner was the first to read aloud her victim statement. She told Boelter she would have opened the door if she were home that day because she trusts law enforcement. Vance Boelter, the man who admitted in court to shooting two Minnesota lawmakers and their spouses, was sentenced to two life terms in prison followed by 40 years Thursday morning.
Judge John R. Tunheim said it was "the longest sentence I have imposed after hearing thousands of cases over the years, but it is well deserved."
Boelter, who turns 59 Thursday, pleaded guilty to six federal charges against him in June. As part of his plea, he confessed to killing former House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband Mark and wounding Sen. John Hoffman and his wife Yvette in a shooting that also targeted their daughter Hope.
The U.S. Department of Justice announced in June it would not seek the death penalty for Boelter.
In a pre-sentencing filing on Tuesday, prosecutors said, "Justice requires that Boelter never be free again." Thursday's sentence carries no possibility of parole.
Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a statement following the sentencing, saying, "This murderer will spend the rest of his life behind bars for his heinous acts of violence against public servants and their families. ... Our hearts remain with the victims' families, loved ones, and all those whose lives were forever changed by these horrific attacks."
The Hennepin County Attorney's Office previously said it plans to move forward with state charges against Boelter: two counts of first-degree premeditated murder, four counts of attempted first-degree murder and one count each of felony cruelty to an animal and impersonating an officer.
The Hoffman family is suing Boelter civilly, accusing him of assault, battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence and negligence per se, according to the complaint.
The June 14, 2025, shootings in the Twin Cities suburbs of Champlin and Brooklyn Park prompted a manhunt that lasted 43 hours and ended in rural Green Isle, Minnesota. Officials said the attacks were politically motivated.
In the most recent legislative session, Hortman's colleagues approved a number of tributes to her, including a memorial garden for the State Office Building and the renaming of Highway 610 and Minnesota's community solar garden program in her honor. Lawmakers also passed two measures championed by Hortman's son Colin, which aim to ease the burdens on families following traumatic events.
Boelter speaks before sentencing
Boelter gave a brief statement to the court before being sentenced.
"To every person I have caused loss, pain, heartache, confusion, shame or loneliness, I am truly sorry," he said.
Hortman children say they still think of parents' murders daily
Sophie and Colin Hortman, children to Melissa and Mark, told the court the pain they experienced after Boelter killed their parents is unforgettable.
"What I cared about in my entire life had been shattered in 30 seconds," Sophie Hortman said. "My parents were dead. The dog had been shot multiple times. My brother was wrecked."
Colin Hortman said he lives with post-traumatic stress disorder.
"The blood that was spilled is the last thing I see before I fall asleep and the first thing I see as I wake," he said, adding that when he pictures his parents, he sees "bullet holes."
Both admitted no penalty would be fully satisfactory, but Colin Hortman asked for the maximum sentence with no possibility of release.
"Justice can never be served for those who lost," Sophie Hortman said. "I miss my mom. I miss my dad. I miss my best friends. I miss believing in the goodness of humanity."
Hoffmans recount horror of shooting, difficulty of aftermath
John Hoffman said he "returned to the Minnesota Senate because I refuse to allow violence to become the author of my future."
Still, he said, his family lives "with a heightened awareness that enters every room before we do."
"Our home no longer feels like the sanctuary it once was," he said. "We installed solid steel doors and reinforced security. Your honor, those aren't home improvements. They are daily reminders that violence followed us home."
Yvette Hoffman said she "genuinely believed" she was dying after being shot.
"I'll never forget looking down and watching my blood stream down that white washing machine as I felt myself sinking to the floor and fading," she said.
"I came face to face with evil," she later added. "I survived it. I will carry the memory of that day with me for the rest of my life."
Hope Hoffman, whose father said her actions "helped save our lives and many others," said she lives not only with the trauma caused by the attack, but that of the "bias and sensationalism" she endured from the media in the aftermath.
"In all reality, I'd like to just be a victim of gun violence who called 911. I really shouldn't have to be advocating for that, but here we are," she said.
Both Hope and Yvette Hoffman shared ill wishes for their attacker.
"Not only is he a criminal and a loser, he's also the worst kind of father he could possibly be," Hope Hoffman said. "I hope one day he miserably dies with that thought."
"If I had a wish, it is when the defendant's life ends, his body is carried out of federal prison in one of those body bags he intended for my family," Yvette Hoffman said.
Fellow lawmakers say attacks shook, changed them
Before the sentencing, Rep. Kristin Bahner, who said Boelter also visited her home the night he shot the Hortmans and Hoffmans, gave an emotional victim impact statement.
"Nothing could prepare me for an assassin at my door," Bahner said. "I never dreamt that doing the job that I love would put my family in harm's way, forever shattering their innocence."
Bahner told the judge, "I only want one thing. That neither courts nor you can give me, Mr. Boelter. I want Melissa back."
Rep. Zack Stephenson, who took over as House DFL leader after Hortman's killing, said Boelter's actions "sent a message of terror to everyone who serves in public life," but that "our caucus is stronger, more unified and even more dedicated to the values that Melissa and Mark lived their life by."
"Melissa consistently acted the way every Minnesotan, every American, would hope their representative would act," Stephenson said. "There has never been another Melissa Hortman and I doubt there ever will be."

Man sentenced to life for shooting 2 Minnesota lawmakers, their spouses
Vance Boelter fatally shot a Minnesota lawmaker and her husband in 2025. He also injured another lawmaker and his wife.
The man who pleaded guilty to federal charges for fatally shooting a Minnesota lawmaker and her husband and the shooting of another lawmaker and his wife was sentenced to life in prison July 23, multiple outlets reported.
Vance Luther Boelter, 58, received two consecutive life sentences, plus 40 years in prison, all to be served consecutively, FOX 9 and The Minnesota Star Tribune reported. The sentence was part of a plea deal that allowed Boelter to avoid the death penalty.
Boelter was handed the sentence just over a year after authorities said he disguised himself as a police officer, fatally shot Minnesota Rep. Melissa Hortman, her husband, Mark, and their dog, then injured State Sen. John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette.
After a massive manhunt, Boelter was arrested and charged with two counts of murder through the use of a firearm, two counts of stalking and firearms offenses for the shootings of the Hortmans and the Hoffmans, and the attempted shooting of the Hoffmans' adult daughter, Hope.
In court on July 23, Boelter, wearing an orange jumpsuit, offered a brief apology.
"To every person I have caused loss, pain, heartache, confusion, sadness, shame or loneliness, I am truly sorry," he said, according to FOX 9.
John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette, who were shot but survived their injuries, addressed Boelter in the courtroom and recounted the attack.
"He looked me in the eyes and pulled the trigger," John Hoffman said in court, according to media reports. "He looked at my wife, Yvette, and pulled the trigger again … Deliberate decisions to end our lives."
Yvette Hoffman said, "I fought him with everything I had and I finally got him out of our home."
"If I had a wish, it is when the defendant’s life ends, his body is carried out of prison in one of those body bags he intended for my family," she added.
Boelter initially pleaded not guilty in August but changed his plea to guilty on all counts on June 11, according to U.S. Attorney for the District of Minnesota Daniel Rosen.
As part of his plea deal, prosecutors agreed not to seek the death penalty and instead asked the court to impose the harshest sentence possible: two consecutive life sentences plus 40 years. In court documents, Boelter's attorneys asked the court to allow him to serve his sentence at a federal prison in Florida.
"Mr. Boelter knows expressing his remorse does not take away the pain he has caused," Boelter's attorneys wrote. "But pleading guilty and agreeing to maximum penalties does show Mr. Boelter’s sincere remorse."
The Hennepin County Attorney's Office said it intends to move forward with state murder charges against Boelter. He is also being sued in civil court by the Hoffman family, according to court documents.
The shootings shocked the nation and were among several attacks that fueled growing concern about political violence in the United States. A month before the shootings in Minnesota, an arsonist firebombed the home of Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. In September, a gunman fatally shot conservative activist Charlie Kirk at an event at Utah Valley University.
After the shootings, the Minnesota State Capitol boosted its security measures, implementing weapons screenings and a second set of detectors for some visitors. Lawmakers also received allowances for home security upgrades and backed plans to fund personal security details. Across the country, states passed legislation to allow candidates to use campaign funds for personal security.
Contributing: Jeanine Santucci

His formal sentence was handed down Thursday morning after more than 90 minutes of emotional statements from the Hortman and Hoffman families and friends.
Boelter did speak briefly, saying only, “To every person I have caused loss, pain, heartache, confusion, sadness, shame or loneliness, I am truly sorry.”
Impact Statements
Hortmans’ son
“In one night, our family went from whole to shattered.”
He described waking up that morning to “a flurry of calls from friends and family” wondering if his parents were alive, and his trying to get details as he continued to get tragic updates.
“Trauma was induced in every person who walked through that house,” he said, saying the image of his parents after they were killed is now the only way he can see them.
“Just resting my head on her shoulder could take the pain away; that was her power. That memory was shot 15 times.”
He said his parents were “the best” a kid could ask for, and his life now “still feels like torture from the violence in my head.”
He then lamented all they — and he — missed out on, before calling for justice to be served.
“My mom will never bake me another cake … She was supposed to bake my wedding cake. That was the one wish that I had.”
“They would have been the best grandparents. They will never meet my children.”
“They would have traveled more, they would have mentored more leaders.”
Hortmans’ daughter
“I’ve written this statement at least once a day for at least a year,” she opened with before starting with their dog, Gilbert, who was also died from the attacks.
She said she didn’t realize Gilbert had been hurt at first, but “looked like he was crying” when he “shakily raised his head” to look at them at the vet. When he died, she described struggled to breathe between sobs.
“What I cared about was that my entire life had just been shattered in 30 seconds. … We had to stand up and keep going.”
Hortmans’ daughter-in-law
She said she won’t dehumanize Boelter because “it’s dehumanization of those you disagree with that brought us here today.”
She described planning to visit Melissa and Mark the day after they killed and everything they looked forward to doing together.
“When I went to bed 404 days ago, every dream … had been shattered.”
She said she still goes to therapy and struggles to discuss their future without getting “physically sick.”
Melissa Hortman’s parents
Her mother highlighted, “My friend, my confidante, my baby,” saying anyone who could do what Boelter did “does not deserve to be any part of a society.”
Her father called Melissa and Mark “two of the most wonderful people in the world,” saying he wishes Boelter would’ve sat down and talked with them.
“The pain is so deep. This is my little girl…” he said before adding, “It is impossible to truly realize the damage that’s been done to our family and to our society.”

The federal sentence is structured to outlast any natural lifespan many times over.

But even two life terms plus 40 years do not finish the legal story.
Minnesota is still waiting.

The federal sentence is severe because the crimes were severe. The remaining state case will now proceed on its own track.

Minnesota has not finished with him yet.

A federal judge sentenced Vance Boelter, 59, to two life terms plus 40 years on Thursday for the June 2025 killings of former Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband Mark, and the near-fatal shooting of state Senator John Hoffman and his wife Yvette.
US District Court Judge John R. Tunheim described it as "the longest sentence I have imposed after hearing thousands of cases over the years, but I do believe it is deserved." Boelter had agreed to plead guilty in June 2026 to avoid the federal death penalty, a deal that drew sharp anger from Mark Hortman's family.
Survivors and family speak in court
According to CNN, Senator Hoffman told the court that he and his wife continue to suffer the physical and psychological toll of that night. "The defendant looked me in the eyes and pulled the trigger. The defendant looked at my wife and chose to do the same," he said. "My wife and I now live with injuries. We live with our bodies remembering the gunfire." His wife Yvette said she had been unable to return to work and attends therapy weekly, adding: "We always have an escape plan now. This isn't how people should live."
The Hortmans' daughter Sophie described grieving her parents alongside their golden retriever Gilbert, who was also shot by Boelter that night. Their son Colin spoke of his parents' absence at his recent wedding. "My days are filled with gray, and the blood that was spilled is the last thing I see before I go to sleep and the first thing I see when I wake," he said. "There is no sentence that weighs 15 gunshots, a murdered dog and the rest of my life."
Melissa Hortman's father, Harold Haluptzok, said the damage extended far beyond the family. "It is impossible to realize the damage that has been done not only to our family, but to our society," he said.
Mark Hortman's sister, Lisa Hortman Bean, voiced frustration at the outcome, saying the arrangement provided Boelter with lifelong accommodation at taxpayers' expense without offering her peace of mind.
How the attack unfolded
Court documents show Boelter arrived at the Hortman home around 3:30 a.m. on June 14, 2025, dressed in a tactical uniform and mask and claiming to be a police officer conducting a welfare check. After Mark Hortman opened the door, Boelter provided a false name and badge number before shooting him multiple times. He then forced his way inside and shot Melissa Hortman as she fled upstairs. Both died.
Boelter had earlier visited the Hoffmans' home that same night and shot the couple inside their house. He also went to two other lawmakers' homes; one family was away on holiday, and at another stop he fled when a passing police officer mistook him for a fellow officer.
Boelter spoke briefly during the hearing, saying:
"To every person I have caused loss, pain, heartache, confusion, sadness, shame, or loneliness, I am truly sorry." His defence attorney said the guilty plea itself demonstrated remorse.

Vance Boelter receives two life terms and 40 years for killing two lawmakers and injuring two others
Vance Boelter, the man who admitted in court to shooting two Minnesota lawmakers and their spouses, was sentenced to two life terms in prison followed by 40 years Thursday morning.
Judge John R. Tunheim said it was “the longest sentence I have imposed after hearing thousands of cases over the years, but it is well deserved.”
Boelter, who turns 59 Thursday, pleaded guilty to six federal charges against him in June. As part of his plea, he confessed to killing former House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband Mark and wounding Sen. John Hoffman and his wife Yvette in a shooting that also targeted their daughter Hope.
The U.S. Department of Justice announced in June it would not seek the death penalty for Boelter.
In a pre-sentencing filing on Tuesday, prosecutors said, “Justice requires that Boelter never be free again.” Thursday’s sentence carries no possibility of parole.
The Hennepin County Attorney’s Office previously said it plans to move forward with state charges against Boelter: two counts of first-degree premeditated murder, four counts of attempted first-degree murder and one count each of felony cruelty to an animal and impersonating an officer.
The Hoffman family is suing Boelter civilly, accusing him of assault, battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence and negligence per se, according to the complaint.
The June 14, 2025, shootings in the Twin Cities suburbs of Champlin and Brooklyn Park prompted a manhunt that lasted 43 hours and ended in rural Green Isle, Minnesota. Officials said the attacks were politically motivated.
In the most recent legislative session, Hortman’s colleagues approved a number of tributes to her, including a memorial garden for the State Office Building and the renaming of Highway 610 and Minnesota’s community solar garden program in her honor. Lawmakers also passed two measures championed by Hortman’s son Colin, which aim to ease the burdens on families following traumatic events.
Boelter speaks before sentencing
Boelter gave a brief statement to the court before being sentenced.
“To every person I have caused loss, pain, heartache, confusion, shame or loneliness, I am truly sorry,” he said.
Hortman children say they still think of parents’ murders daily
Sophie and Colin Hortman, children to Melissa and Mark, told the court the pain they experienced after Boelter killed their parents is unforgettable.
“What I cared about is my entire life had been shattered in 30 seconds,” Sophie Hortman said. “My parents were dead. The dog had been shot multiple times. My brother was wrecked.”
Colin Hortman said he lives with post-traumatic stress disorder.
“The blood that was spilled is the last thing I see before I fall asleep and the first thing I see as I wake,” he said, adding that when he pictures his parents, he sees “bullet holes.”
Both admitted no penalty would be fully satisfactory, but Colin Hortman asked for the maximum sentence with no possibility of release.
“Justice can never be served for those who lost,” Sophie Hortman said. “I miss my mom. I miss my dad. I miss my best friends. I miss believing in the goodness of humanity.”
Hoffmans recount horror of shooting, difficulty of aftermath
John Hoffman said he “returned to the Minnesota Senate because I refuse to allow violence to become the author of my future.”
Still, he said, his family lives “with a heightened awareness that enters every room before we do.”
“Our home no longer feels like the sanctuary it once was,” he said. “We installed solid steel doors and reinforced security. Your honor, those aren’t home improvements. They are daily reminders that violence followed us home.”
Yvette Hoffman said she “genuinely believed” she was dying after being shot.
“I’ll never forget looking down and watching my blood stream down that white washing machine as I felt myself sinking to the floor and fading,” she said.
“I came face to face with evil,” she later added. “I survived it. I will carry the memory of that day with me for the rest of my life.”
Hope Hoffman, whose father said her actions “helped save our lives and many others,” said she lives not only with the trauma caused by the attack, but that of the “bias and sensationalism” she endured from the media in the aftermath.
“In all reality, I’d like to just be a victim of gun violence who called 911. I really shouldn’t have to be advocating for that, but here we are,” she said.
Both Hope and Yvette Hoffman shared ill wishes for their attacker.
“Not only is he a criminal and a loser, he’s also the worst kind of father he could possibly be,” Hope Hoffman said. “I hope one day he miserably dies with that thought.”
“If I had a wish, it is when the defendant’s life ends, his body is carried out of federal prison in one of those body bags he intended for my family,” Yvette Hoffman said.
Fellow lawmakers say attacks shook, changed them
Before the sentencing, Rep. Kristin Bahner, who said Boelter also visited her home the night he shot the Hortmans and Hoffmans, gave an emotional victim impact statement.
“Nothing could prepare me for an assassin at my door,” Bahner said. “I never dreamt that doing the job that I love would put my family in harm’s way, forever shattering their innocence.”
Bahner told the judge, “I only want one thing. That neither courts nor you can give me, Mr. Boelter. I want Melissa back.”
Rep. Zack Stephenson, who took over as House DFL leader after Hortman’s killing, said Boelter’s actions “sent a message of terror to everyone who serves in public life,” but that “our caucus is stronger, more unified and even more dedicated to the values that Melissa and Mark lived their life by.”
“Melissa consistently acted the way every Minnesotan, every American, would hope their representative would act,” Stephenson said. “There has never been another Melissa Hortman and I doubt there ever will be.”

Boelter attempted to kill the Hoffmans’ daughter and Rep. Kristin Bahner, who was not at her Maple Grove home when he arrived.
